title: The principles of war
note: US Army doctrine (FM 3-0) lists nine principles of war: objective, offensive, mass, economy of force, maneuver, unity of command, security, surprise and simplicity, often remembered as MOOSEMUSS. They distill historically successful operations; doctrine stresses they are tools for judgment and analysis, not a checklist.

read.title: Nine principles, one judgment
text: The US Army lists nine principles of war. Objective comes first: every operation must aim at a clear, decisive and attainable goal that serves the political purpose of the war. Offensive means seizing and keeping the initiative, so the enemy must react rather than act. Mass concentrates the effects of combat power where and when they decide the issue, and economy of force is its partner: spend the minimum on secondary efforts so the main effort gets the maximum, deliberately accepting risk elsewhere.

Maneuver places the enemy at a disadvantage through flexible movement and fire. Unity of command gives each objective one responsible commander. Security keeps the enemy from gaining surprise, while surprise strikes the enemy at a time, place or manner he has not prepared for. Simplicity asks for clear, uncomplicated plans, because the more complicated a plan, the more it suffers from friction.

Doctrine traces the list to the British officer J. F. C. Fuller and insists it is not a checklist. The principles pull against each other: massing for the main blow weakens security somewhere else. Their value lies in helping commanders, and students of history, ask the right questions about why operations succeed or fail.
